questions.question: Calculate specificity of '#nav .item a':
questions.explanation: #nav = 1 ID (0,1,0,0), .item = 1 class (0,0,1,0), a = 1 element (0,0,0,1). Summed tuple = (0,1,1,1).

questions.question: Higher specificity always beats lower even if the lower rule is:
questions.explanation: Specificity outranks source order: a more specific selector wins regardless of where it appears (unless !important enters).

questions.question: Calculate 'ul li span' vs 'ul .item span':

options.text: ul .item span wins (0,0,1,2) vs ul li span (0,0,0,3)

questions.explanation: ul .item span = 1 class + 2 elements (0,0,1,2) beats ul li span = 3 elements (0,0,0,3) because classes outrank elements.

questions.question: p:hover has specificity (0,0,1,1) because:
questions.explanation: :hover is a pseudo-class (class tier). p:hover = element + pseudo-class = (0,0,1,1).

questions.question: Two rules with (0,2,0,1) and (0,1,3,0): which wins?

options.text: (0,2,0,1) — it has more classes (2 > 1), compared at the class tier first

questions.explanation: Compare tier by tier: class tier 2 vs 1 decides; element counts only matter if classes tie.

questions.question: Inline style contributes to which tuple position?
questions.explanation: Inline styles sit in the highest (a) position of (a,b,c,d), beating IDs, classes, and elements.

questions.question: The mnemonic 'ID=100, Class=10, Element=1' is a simplification of:

options.text: Comparing tiers left-to-right (not real base-10 addition)
Actual base-10 math you can sum

questions.explanation: The 100/10/1 heuristic helps intuition but specificity compares tier-by-tier; 11 elements (0,0,0,11) still lose to 1 class (0,0,1,0).

questions.question: To make a rule win without !important and without an ID, you can:

options.text: Add a class or element to raise its specificity above the competitor

questions.explanation: Increment the class/element tier intentionally (e.g. repeat a class or add an ancestor) to outrank the other rule cleanly.
